parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -algia.

parole.significato: acalypha (any plant of the genus Acalypha)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Acalypha, from Ancient Greek ἀκαλύφη (akalúphē).

Borrowed from New Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught; from the name of the supposed former owner of that estate, the Attica hero Akademos.

parole.significato: pheasant's eye (plant of the genus Adonis)
parole.testo: From New Latin Adonis, from Ancient Greek Ἄδωνις (Ádōnis).
From New Latin aphēlium, from Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “from, away from”) "from, away from" + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “the Sun”), modeled after apogaeum.
From New Latin Agave, from Ancient Greek Ἀγαυή (Agauḗ), name of one of the daughters of Cadmus, from ἀγαυός (agauós, “noble, illustrious”).

parole.significato: candlenut (any plant of the genus Aleurites)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Aleurites, from Ancient Greek ἀλευρίτης (aleurítēs, “made of wheat flour”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἁμαμηλίς (hamamēlís, “possibly the medlar”).

parole.significato: bowfin (freshwater fish of the family Amiidae)
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀμία (amía).
From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós). By surface analysis, ana- (“reversal”) + cron(o-) (“time”) + -ismo (“-ism”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀνδρήνη (andrḗnē, “wasp”).
From New Latin anthēra, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρά (anthērá), feminine form of ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”) from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower, blossom”).
Unadapted borrowing from New Latin argon, from Ancient Greek ἀργόν (argón), substantivized neuter form of ἀργός (argós, “idle, lazy”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀσκαρίς (askarís, “an intestinal worm”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος (azaléos, “dry”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “small staff”), from βακτηρία (baktēría) + -ium.

parole.significato: palmyra palm (tree of the genus Borassus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Borassus, derived from Ancient Greek βόρασσος (bórassos).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek βροντή (brontḗ, “thunder”) + σαυρος (sauros, “lizard”).

parole.significato: cockatiel (a small, rather atypical cockatoo with a distinctive pointed yellow crest)
parole.testo: From New Latin calopsittacus, from Ancient Greek καλός (kalós, “beautiful, lovely”) + ψιττακός (psittakós, “parrot”). Compare Portuguese calopsita.
Learned borrowing from New Latin catharticus, from Ancient Greek καθαρτικός (kathartikós).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos) "hollow" + ἄκανθα (ákantha) "spine".
Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.
From New Latin cirrhosis, from Ancient Greek κῐρρός (kĭrrhós) and -ωσις (-ōsis) (Italian -osi).
Borrowed from New Latin cladus, from Ancient Greek κλάδος (kládos, “branch”).
From New Latin, from Latin clēmatis, from Ancient Greek κληματίς (klēmatís, “brushwood, clematis”), from κλῆμα (klêma, “vine, branch with vines”).
From New Latin chlorum, from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”).
Borrowed from New Latin coccus, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek κολοβός (kolobós, “maimed”).
From New Latin Corchorus, from Ancient Greek κόρχορος (kórkhoros).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús, “hairy, shaggy, dense”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).
New Latin, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís, “dolphin”) because of their flower shape, thought to resemble a back of a dolphin.
From New Latin Dermestes, from Ancient Greek δερμηστής (dermēstḗs).
From New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”).
From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).

From epiglottide, from New Latin epiglottis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís), derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, epiglottid(e) (“epiglottis”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).
Borrowed from New Latin aethalium, derived from Ancient Greek αἴθαλος (aíthalos, “soot”).
From New Latin exaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἐξαίρεσῐς (exaíresĭs, “a taking out, an extraction”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φακός (phakós, “lens”) + χοῖρος (khoîros, “pig”).
From New Latin, from Latin Phaethon, from Ancient Greek Φαέθων (Phaéthōn).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φλέως (phléōs, “wool-tufted reed”).
From New Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “light-bearing”).

From glottide, from New Latin glottis, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís), derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, glottid(e) (“glottis”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).
From New Latin glottidem, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).

parole.significato: gorgonian, sea whip, sea fan (cnidarian of order Alcyonacea, syn. Gorgonacea)
parole.testo: From New Latin Gorgonia, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ).
From New Latin Hydrastis, from Ancient Greek ὑδράστινα (hudrástina, “kind of hemp”).

parole.significato: a dermatosis characterized by the presence of vesicles and blisters
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hydroa, derived from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).
Borrowed from New Latin hypanthium, derived from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).
From New Latin Hypericum, from Ancient Greek ὑπερικόν (huperikón).
Borrowed from New Latin Hippomane, from Ancient Greek ἱππομανές (hippomanés, “thorn-apple”).

From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”). By surface analysis, isco- + -emia.
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek Λυκαων (Lukaōn, “a name”), λυκαων (lukaōn), from λυκάνθρωπος (lukánthrōpos, “werewolf, wolf-man”).
From New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”).
Borrowed from New Latin megalopa, derived from Ancient Greek μεγάλος (megálos, “big, great”) + ὤψ, ὠπός (ṓps, ōpós, “appearance”).
New Latin, from Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “large”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”), in reference to its flippers.
Borrowed from New Latin mesonephros, derived from Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”).
Borrowed from New Latin metanephros, derived from Ancient Greek νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”).
New Latin, from Ancient Greek, from Ancient Greek stem of μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) + stem of οὖς (oûs, “ear”), from the shape of the leaves.
From New Latin Miscanthus, from Ancient Greek μίσχος (mískhos, “petiole”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).
From New Latin neon, from Ancient Greek νέον (néon), neuter form of νέος (néos, “new”).
From New Latin nystagmus, from Ancient Greek νυσταγμός (nustagmós, “nodding, drowsiness”), from νυστάζω (nustázō, “nod, be sleepy”).
Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
Borrowed from New Latin ooecium, derived from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”) + οἰκίον (oikíon, “dwelling”).
From New Latin ophiurus (“brittle star”), from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “serpent”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) (referring to the serpent-like arms of the brittle star).
Borrowed from New Latin opisthonephros, derived from Ancient Greek ὄπισθεν (ópisthen, “behind”) + νεφρός (nephrós, “kidney”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (órux).
From New Latin oryctēropūs, from Ancient Greek ὀρυκτήρ (oruktḗr, “miner, digger”) + πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: star-of-Bethlehem, any of various perennial plants of the genus Ornithogalum
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Ornithogalum, itself from Ancient Greek ὀρνῑθόγαλον (ornīthógalon), a compound of ὄρνις (órnis, “bird”) + γάλα (gála, “milk”).
Borrowed from New Latin osphradium, derived from the root of Ancient Greek ὀσφραίνομαι (osphraínomai, “I perceive a smell”).
Borrowed from New Latin Palladium, named after the asteroid 2 Pallas, named after Ancient Greek Παλλάς (Pallás) (see Etymology 1).
Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek παραμήκης (paramḗkēs, “oblong, oval”) + -ium.
Borrowed from New Latin perichaetium, derived from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “about”) + χαίτη (khaítē, “flowing hair, foliage”).
From New Latin, from Latin Pieris, from Ancient Greek Πιερίς (Pierís, “a Muse”), first worshiped in Πιερία (Piería, “Pieria”).
Borrowed from New Latin pygidium, from Ancient Greek πυγή (pugḗ, “tail”).

parole.significato: any bird of the genus Pipra
parole.testo: From New Latin Pipra, from Ancient Greek πίπρα (pípra, “kind of woodpecker”).
Borrowed from New Latin pyreticus, from Ancient Greek πυρετικός (puretikós, “febrile”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: a member of the Pythium taxonomic genus, of molds.
parole.testo: From New Latin pȳthium, derived from Ancient Greek πῡ́θω (pū́thō, “to (cause to) putrefy”).
Borrowed from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta (“cake”), from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta, “flat”).
Borrowed from New Latin podetium, derived from the ποδ- (pod-) stem of Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “in place of”) + κύων (kúōn, “dog”).
Borrowed from New Latin Protista, from Ancient Greek πρώτιστος (prṓtistos), corresponding to proto- + -ista.
From New Latin pteryla, derived from Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing; feather”) + ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “forest”).
Borrowed from New Latin ptilōsis, from the Ancient Greek πτῐ́λωσῐς (ptĭ́lōsĭs).
From New Latin rhachis, -is, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “spine, ridge”), with an unetymological -id- added to the stem.
From New Latin rhēsus, arbitrary formation from Latin Rhēsus, from Ancient Greek Ῥῆσος (Rhêsos), mythical Thracian king.
Semi-learned borrowing from New Latin rhodium, from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”).
From New Latin Schistosoma, from Ancient Greek roots. By surface analysis, schisto- + -soma.
Borrowed from New Latin selēnium, from Ancient Greek Σελήνη (Selḗnē, “moon”).
Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma).
From New Latin sōrus, from Ancient Greek σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).
From New Latin spagiria, spagyria, coined from Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō, “to draw, pull”) + ἀγείρω (ageírō, “to assemble”).
From New Latin spasmodicus, from Ancient Greek σπασμώδης (spasmṓdēs, “spasmodic”), from σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”).
Borrowed from New Latin spermatium, derived from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed”).
From New Latin splanchnicus, from Ancient Greek σπλαγχνικός (splankhnikós), from σπλάγχνα (splánkhna, “viscera”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek στέγος (stégos, “roof”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).
From New Latin Thalictrum, from Latin thalictrum, ultimately from Ancient Greek θάλικτρον (tháliktron, “meadowrue”).

Borrowed from New Latin therapeuticus (“curing, healing”), from Ancient Greek θεραπευτικός (therapeutikós, “attentive, helpful, obliging, curative”), from θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs, “one who waits on another, an attendant”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “I wait on, attend, serve, cure”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τύφη (túphē, “a species of cattail”).
From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “tyrant”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).

New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρί-, stem of τρεῖς (treîs, “three”) + κέρατ-, stem of κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “face”). The nonstandard pronunciation *triceratòpo is due to influence of topo ("mouse").
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρίχινος (tríkhinos, “of hair”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).
Borrowed from New Latin Trichophyton, from Ancient Greek θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant; creature”). By surface analysis, trico- + -fito.
Borrowed from New Latin Trichoglossus, from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, trico- + -glosso.
New Latin, from Derived from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “borer”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”), because of their corkscrew-like motion.
From New Latin, alteration of Uromastix, from Ancient Greek οὐρά (ourá, “a tail”) + μάστιξ (mástix, “a scourge, a whip”).

From New Latin Utopia, the name of a fictional island, possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not, no”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”).
From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ζα (za) (from διά (diá, “through, across”)) + γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).
Borrowed from New Latin zooecium, derived from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).
